prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, which brought frequency standards to the 10^-18 level of uncertainty and opened new precision tests of fundamental physics

statement.case_for: Having read all eight ballots, I move my preferred configuration from B022 to B025. The optical lattice clock is the one shortlisted candidate that every member ranked (eight of eight, two first places, four top-three placements), and the support is not an artefact of a shared habit: members from atomic physics, condensed matter, particle physics and astroparticle physics each describe the same facts independently. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes the trade-off between atom number and motional or light-shift systematics, and the resulting clocks reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, are reproduced and intercompared in several national laboratories, and underpin tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and the discussed redefinition of the second. The invention criterion is met cleanly, the two-name attribution (Katori for the concept and first realisation, Ye for taking accuracy, stability and many-body clock physics to the limit) is compact and is accepted without dispute by all eight proposers, and no maturity doubt is raised by anyone. As a statistical physicist I also value that the many-body and spin-exchange aspects of the lattice clock are now physics in their own right, not only metrology.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this is an instrument and metrology prize rather than the discovery of a new phenomenon, and the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 prize for trapped-ion control already cover the neighbouring ground, so the committee must articulate what is new in the lattice clock. There is also a real attribution question about Lemonde, Takamoto and others in the early lattice-clock work, and about a possible overlap with the thorium nuclear clock that Danielsson raised. Finally, choosing it over magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene means giving priority to maturity over the larger conceptual opening, which is a judgment I am making with some reluctance.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle graphene (B022) fourth because the origin of the superconductivity and the full phase diagram are still debated, so the interpretation is not yet stable and the timing is somewhat early.
responses.response: This is the point that moved me most. I still think the phenomenology (flat bands, correlated insulators, superconducting domes) is secure and reproduced across many moire systems, so the discovery is not in doubt, and I would not call it premature in the sense that the effect might disappear. But Eriksson is right that a citation for B022 would have to avoid saying anything about mechanism, and that it is only about eight years since the experiments. Where I disagree is on B029, which Eriksson ranks first: I accept its maturity and the clean link to electronic-structure theory, but only two members ranked it and the MgO step is shared with groups outside the credited names, so I do not see it ahead of the clocks.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube (B007) first as the opening of a genuine new observational window, while conceding that source identification is still thin (one blazar at about 3 sigma and Galactic-plane evidence).
responses.response: I agree that the diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux is a real discovery and I ranked it sixth for that reason, not because I doubt it. My qualification is the one Pearce raises himself: the discovery of the diffuse flux is firm but the astronomy that would make the case vivid (identified sources) is still thin, and the AMANDA and Baikal lineage makes the two-name attribution contestable against the IceCube collaboration. If the committee wants a discovery of a new phenomenon rather than a measurement tool, B007 is a serious alternative, but I would want to see the source evidence strengthen before preferring it to a well-confirmed clock.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the lattice clock first on the strength of the atomic-structure and polarizability underpinnings of the magic wavelength, and regards recognition as timely, arguably overdue, while noting that the frequency comb prize (2005) covers the enabling tool.
responses.response: I agree with her on maturity and on the two-name attribution, and her point about independent confirmation at JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, SYRTE and PTB is exactly what a prize citation needs. I would add one qualification: because the comb prize already honoured the enabling tool, the citation should be phrased around the magic-wavelength lattice concept and its realisation at the 1e-18 level, not around precision spectroscopy in general. On B022 she keeps MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero only and drops Bistritzer, which I think is a harder cut than the other proposers make, since Bistritzer is first author of the 2011 prediction.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B016) first as the architecture underlying superconducting quantum processors, and sees it as following naturally from the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in circuits.
responses.response: I take the impact argument seriously, but I ranked B016 outside my top eight and am unmoved on two points. Only four members ranked it, with three different laureate sets across the proposers, so the attribution (Blais against Wallraff against Girvin) is unsettled. And the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits makes the distinct scope harder to justify than Johansson suggests, which Kroll also noted. I would also keep B037 ahead of it, since the optical-lattice simulators have a more direct line to many-body and statistical physics.

uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers an instrument-level prize (B025) to a new-phenomenon prize (B022, B007) in this cycle, given the recent AMO precedents of 2005, 2012 and 2025.
Whether Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow or Hinkley should be weighed against the two-person attribution.
Whether a thorium nuclear clock claim would overlap with Ye's part of the credit within the next few years.
For the fallback B022, whether Bistritzer should be credited alongside MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, and how to treat Cao and other experimental authors.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. I have no documented connection to Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Bistritzer, and my listed co-authors and institutions do not overlap with the shortlisted credited names.
